en: The Chapter on the Secret Essential Method for the Birth of the Eight Great Youthful Attendants from the Single Syllable of the Holy Immovable Honored One,
composed by the Translation Bureau of Daxingshan Temple.
Vajrapāṇi said:
"The mental conceptions of all sentient beings differ;
they may be either favorable or adverse."
Therefore, the Tathāgata manifests bodies of both compassion and wrath to bring about benefit accordingly.
The commentary explains:
Because the Buddhas possess great compassion and pity for sentient beings,
they exhort those who are compliant by means of compliance,
and they restrain those who are resistant by means of resistance.
When one Buddha abides in the samādhi of wrath,
all Buddhas of the ten directions likewise enter the samādhi of wrathful anger.
Is it not that Vairocana manifests as a Vidyārāja within the signless?
At that time, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas no longer manifest wrathful bodies.
Therefore, the Tathāgatas of the four directions manifest the bodies of *ājñā-kāya* (commanding forms) to subdue all Māras.
Although they still do not personally follow [the practitioner],
this is because their original vows differ;
or it may be Trailokyavijaya Bodhisattva.
He subdues the celestial Māras and the greed, hatred, and delusion of the three periods of time;
or, as Mañjuśrī, he tames the ever-attendant Māra known as Vināyaka.
And human māras, or Yama-mṛtyukas;
subduing nāga-māras and all hostile enemies,
or vajra-yakṣas.
He subdues ghosts, demons, and the ignorant;
such various [deeds] cannot be fully described.
Acala Vidyārāja constantly follows the practitioner.
All obstacles created by devas, vināyakas,
nāgas, or ghosts shall be simultaneously extinguished.
However, if all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas were to dwell together in a single samādhi,
there could be those who follow the emissaries of their unwavering great vows.
Thereupon, the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra was able to penetrate and clarify the Way;
he then opened and examined the essential texts of the Secret Treasury and discovered the single-syllable heart-mantra of the Vidyārāja Acala.
One should adorn a single syllable with eight syllables;
these eight syllables constitute the phrase of taking refuge.
The syllable *Haṃ* is the primary deity.
If that is so, why are the first eight characters above devoid of their forms?
For what reason? Because the eight characters beginning with *na* and *mo* [are as follows].
Each and every one returns its homage to the single syllable HAṂ. Therefore,
from those eight syllables, the messengers of homage are produced,
surrounding the primary deity HAṂ.
Thus, there are eight great youths.
First is the Bodhisattva Jñānaprabha-vajramegha (Wisdom-Light Vajra-Cloud).
He is called "Turning Back the Light" because he uses wisdom-light to illuminate and turn back all things.
Second is the Bodhisattva Prajñānanda-vajra;
"Prajñānanda" means that wisdom is transformed into joy.
Third is the Bodhisattva Anavatapta.
Fourth is the Bodhisattva Caturangula;
fifth is Ukkoṭaka;
sixth is the Pure Bhikṣu.
Seventh is Kaṅkara;
eighth is Cchataka.
These messengers correspond to the four wisdoms and the four pāramitās.
In order to personally follow and comply with the commands of Mahāvairocana,
they manifest these forms to surround the noble Acala;
the meaning of each is revealed within their respective mantras.
The commentary states:
The Eastern Vajra Family is the gateway of bodhicitta.
Using sunlight as a metaphor,
the messenger who emerges is named Wisdom Light (Prajñāprabha).
The Jewel Family of the South is the Gate of Merit.
Therefore, the messenger who is born is named Hui-xi (Joy of Wisdom).
This is because she takes joy in the two adornments of merit and wisdom.
The Western Lotus Family is precisely the gateway of wisdom.
The reason the messenger appears is that his name is Anavatapta,
which translates as "Without Heat.
This signifies that the lotus grows from the waters of a pond that is pure and free from defilement.
The northern Karma family is the gate of diligence;
thus, the messengers produced from it are named "Fingered Virtue" (Aṅgulīśa).
This present family points to the virtues of the three preceding families.
Because one can attain the fruit by relying on diligence, it is called "Pointing to Virtue.
The four aforementioned wisdoms—the Vajra Pāramitās—are the practice of bodhicitta;
therefore, they appear.
The messenger is named Ukupāga,
which in this language means "Transcending Abiding in the World.
He is the one whose mental conduct consists of the merit of the Jewel Perfection.
Therefore, the messenger who brings forth [this teaching] is named the Pure Bhikṣu.
This signifies that the bhikṣu is able to protect the Jewel of the Dharma.
The practice of the perfection of Dharma consists of the conduct of compassion.
Therefore, the messenger who appears is named Kaṅkara,
which translates as "Conformity.
The perfection of action (karmapāramitā) is precisely the mental conduct of skillful means (upāya).
For this reason, the messenger who brings forth [the result] is named Citra;
this is translated here as "Averting Calamity" (Sīhara).
It is because the Bodhisattva, through skillful means (*upāya*), manifests a form of wrath.
The exposition on the bases of the eight youths is hereby concluded.
If a practitioner wishes to attain the siddhis of the present or the future,
they should invoke the respective names of those [deities] within the performance of the ritual.
Please grant protection and perform mudrās while reciting mantras;
this shall immediately accomplish all the most excellent siddhis of the world.
The mantra of the Bodhisattva Prajñāprabha-kumāra is as follows: join the vajra palms with the *aṅguṣṭha* (thumb) and *tarjanī* (index finger) joined like a needle.
Oṃ vajramate jvala bodhicittaya namaḥ. The mantra of the Honored One, Prajñāratī Bodhisattva, is: Hold the golden vessel with the seal of patience, in the form of a jewel.
Oṃ ratnā-mate sma-ha-mahā-maṇi. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Anavatapta is: "The golden vessel, with the patience of the wish-fulfilling gem, is like a lotus leaf."

Oṃ namo sarvabodhisattvānāṃ mahādharmadāmodara. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta for taking refuge in the Honored One is as follows: Join the palms with the right hand placed over the left, and bring the faces together.
Oṃ karama mahāve-riye pūrapūra-kāmaṃ namo bhagavate kumāra-rājasya. The mantra of the Youthful Lord is as follows: [Perform] the vajra-palms gesture.
Oṃ mahākārya-ta. This is the mantra for the messenger of the pure bhikṣu who takes refuge in the Honored One; it is accompanied by the *brahmapustaka-mudrā* (the seal of the sacred scripture).
Oṃ maṇi viśuddha-vadana-kurukullā-ṛkṣa-vadana. (Homage to the deity; the mantra of the youth Krodhakumāra is as follows: join the hands in the lotus gesture.)
Oṃ dāruṇa karkaṭe tiṣṭha vajra. The mantra for the deity Krodhakumāra is as follows: Form the outer five-pronged mudrā.
Oṃ karmamūla cetaya ka hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ na. Next, for the mantra of the principal deity, use the mudrā commonly employed in the sūtras.
Oṃ ācara zaṇa haṃ. Next, the ritual for the image is explained.
The practitioner should select a pure and quiet location.
Do not allow humans or non-humans to see it.
Then, the practitioner, together with the artisans, shall purify themselves and don new, clean garments.
They should take white cotton wool, or a clean board, or a clean cloth.
Have the principal deity painted according to the image found in the *Sūtra Common to the Eight Great Krodhas*,
with the form of Prajñāloka:
slightly wrathful and wearing a celestial crown.
The body is white-yellow in color;
the right hand holds a five-pronged wisdom vajra,
and the left hand rests upon a moon disc atop a lotus.
Adorned with various ornaments such as the *kāṣāya* robe and necklaces,
next is the Bodhisattva Prajñānanda;
his form resembles that of Maitreya, and his face displays a smiling expression.
Her complexion is like a red lotus;
her left hand holds a maṇi jewel,
and her right hand holds a trident hook.
The Bodhisattva Anavatapta has a form like that of Brahmā;
his complexion is like pure gold, he wears a garuḍa upon his crown,
and in his left hand he holds a lotus flower.
He holds a single-pronged vajra in his right hand and rides upon a nāga king;
Bodhisattva Indradeva has the appearance of a yakṣa.
His body is like space, and he has three eyes; he is clad in armor,
holds a wheel in his left hand,
and a trident spear in his right hand.
He wears a five-pronged crown of *ukūpagada*,
manifests a fierce and wrathful appearance, his body is golden in color,
and his right hand holds a *vajra*.
The left hand forms the fist-seal (*muṣṭi-mudrā*).
The pure bhikṣu has his hair and beard shaven and wears the dharma-kāṣāya.
A sash is tied over the left shoulder;
the left hand holds a *brahmapustaka* (palm-leaf manuscript),
and the right hand, held at the heart, grasps a five-pronged vajra.
His right shoulder was exposed,
and he wore a crimson lower garment around his waist;
his facial features were neither young nor old.
Her eyes are like blue lotuses;
her upper teeth protrude over her lower ones.
Next is Siṃhakarṇī, whose form is like that of a fifteen-year-old child.
He wears a lotus-flower crown and his body is white in color;
his two hands are joined in *añjali*,
with the space between his two thumbs and index fingers [open].
A vajra is inserted crosswise;
he is adorned with celestial robes and subtle ornaments.
Next, Citta is also like a youth.
The form is like a red lotus, with five topknots tied: one at the crown of the head,
one on the forehead,
and two on the left and right sides of the head.
After performing the single-vertex binding,
one represents the five directions and five wisdoms; the left hand holds a *vajra*,
and the right hand grasps a vajra-staff.
Because those of a wrathful mind and evil nature do not wear the *kāṣāya*,
they wrap celestial garments around their necks and shoulders.
This concludes the explanation of the method for painting the image.
Next, the method of making offerings is explained.
When a practitioner wishes to present an offering,
they must first generate the bodhicitta.
What is the bodhicitta?
It refers to the resolve to rescue sentient beings;
it is the thought of bringing them relief that arises upon contemplating the suffering and afflictions of sentient beings.
At the time of generating the mind of awakening in this manner,
Acala Vidyārāja and the eight great youths emerge from one's own mind as uninvited teachers to protect and sustain the practitioner.
One should make offerings while dwelling in a quiet place within a mountain forest,
burning incense, scattering flowers, and reciting the mantra.
When practicing in this manner,
the messengers will manifest their forms and serve according to one's wishes.
First, one must pay homage to the Tathāgatas of the four directions and make great vows.
He immediately prostrated toward the east and made this vow:
"I vow to deliver boundless sentient beings.
This is the vow of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
This is the gateway of the bodhicitta.
Since the bodhicitta is the mind that delivers sentient beings,
those who give rise to this vow and pay homage [do so for this reason].
Until one attains Buddhahood, may one always receive the empowerment of Vajrasattva,
causing the bodhicitta to be perfected.
Next, prostrate toward the south and reflect as follows:
The vow to gather boundless merit and wisdom is the cause of the Wisdom of Equality;
it is the gateway of merit and wisdom.
Because they benefit sentient beings through the two provisions of merit and wisdom,
those who make this vow and perform this prostration will,
until they reach the stage of Buddhahood, constantly receive the empowerment conferred by the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja at each successive level.
With merit and wisdom perfected,
next prostrate toward the western direction and make this vow:
"I vow to study the boundless Dharma gates."
This vow is the cause of the wisdom of wondrous observation;
it is the gateway of wisdom,
for the sake of becoming a great Dharma King.
Those who make this vow and pay homage shall,
until they attain Buddhahood, receive the empowerment of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and achieve the perfection of wisdom.
Next, one pays homage to the North and forms this thought:
"The Tathāgata’s boundless vow is the cause of the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done."
This is the gateway of performing actions,
because one performs all manner of activities before the Buddhas.
If one makes this vow while prostrating, [the merit is immeasurable].
Until the attainment of Buddhahood, one shall receive the empowerment of the Bodhisattva Vajrakarma and accomplish vast activities of offering within all Buddha-worlds.
Next, one should prostrate to the Tathāgata Vairocana and speak these words:
"I vow to realize unsurpassed bodhi.
This is the cause for the Wisdom of the Essential Nature of the Dharma-realm.
It is the realization of the stage of Mahāvairocana Samantabhadra.
Pervading the entire dharma-realm,
he made this vow for the sake of further benefiting sentient beings.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions simultaneously bore witness to it.
He praised him, saying, "Excellent!
Therefore, all the noble assemblies of bodhisattvas shall together protect him;
before long, he shall attain the Unsurpassed Way.
Having thus stated the general vows,
one should now set forth the remaining specific vows according to one's inclination,
dedicating these roots of virtue toward the equal benefit of both oneself and others.
Furthermore, they do not consume impure things;
their minds are free from sorrow, and they do not give rise to afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion.
Taking no pleasure in worldly delights, they cultivate meditative concentration deeply.
A practitioner who acts in this way experiences the great bliss of the world;
they are a teacher to sentient beings,
and samādhi manifests before them.
May one swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

This is the chapter on the secret essential dharma of the eight great youths born from the single syllable of the Noble Immovable Lord (Acalanātha). Recorded on the twenty-eighth day of Qingming in the year of the Water-Hare (Bimao), the twenty-second year of the Kenpō era.
I have humbly annotated the Master’s transmission and published it; however,
as there were no alternative versions available for collation, I have recorded it as such,
noting that my hair has not yet been bound in the formal cap of adulthood.
This is prepared for future generations to evaluate and adopt or reject;
I hope it may serve as a definitive standard.
Written by the monk Mudo of Ryūge on Mount Hō in the Land of the Sun (Japan).
